# Australia Property Market Profile

## Structural Characteristics
- Population: ~27M, highly urbanized (Sydney ~5.3M, Melbourne ~5.1M, Brisbane ~2.6M)
- Housing stock: ~11M dwellings
- Owner-occupation rate: ~67%
- Dominant housing type: Standalone houses (70%+), apartments growing in Sydney/Melbourne
- Key institutions: CoreLogic (data), RBA (macroprudential), APRA (banking regulator), State Revenue Offices (stamp duty)

## Historical Cycle Phases

| Period | Phase | Real Price Change | Key Driver |
|--------|-------|------------------|------------|
| 1996-2003 | Boom | +80% | Financial deregulation, investor boom, CGT discount (1999) |
| 2004-2008 | Boom (slowing) | +20% | Mining boom, immigration, credit expansion |
| 2009-2012 | Correction/Flat | -5% then flat | GFC then mining boom support |
| 2013-2017 | Boom | +50% (Sydney +75%) | Investor boom, IO lending, foreign buying |
| 2018-2019 | Correction | -10% (Sydney -15%) | APRA macroprudential, Royal Commission credit crunch |
| 2020-2022 | Boom | +30% | COVID stimulus, record-low rates, HomeBuilder |
| 2022-2024 | Correction | -5 to -10% | RBA aggressive hiking (0.10% → 4.35%) |
| 2024-2025 | Stabilization | Flat to +3% | Rate peak, supply shortage, migration surge |

## Key Macro Drivers (AU Specific)

### 1. Mortgage Rate Structure — Variable Dominance
- ~85% of mortgages are variable rate (unique among DM)
- RBA rate changes transmit to households within 1-2 months
- Fastest monetary policy transmission in the OECD
- "Mortgage cliff": fixed-rate roll-offs (2023-2024) from 2% to 6%+

### 2. Negative Gearing + CGT Discount
- Negative gearing: rental losses deductible against other income
- CGT discount: 50% discount if held > 12 months
- Combined: powerful tax incentive for leveraged property investment
- ~2.2M Australians own investment property (~20% of taxpayers)
- Reform politically toxic (2019 election lost on this platform)

### 3. Foreign Buyer Rules
- Foreign buyers limited to new builds (not existing dwellings)
- FIRB approval required + application fees + stamp duty surcharges
- Chinese buying surged 2013-2017, declined since (capital controls + FIRB fees)
- Temporary residents can buy one existing dwelling (must sell on departure)

### 4. Supply Constraints
- Chronic undersupply (estimated 100-200K dwelling deficit)
- Zoning restrictions, NIMBYism, slow approvals
- Construction costs +25% since 2019
- Builder insolvencies surging (fixed-price contracts + cost inflation)
- National Housing Accord: target 1.2M new homes over 5 years (widely seen as unachievable)

### 5. Migration
- Record net overseas migration ~500K/year (2023-2024)
- International students = major rental demand driver
- 70% of migrants settle in Sydney or Melbourne

## Key Data Sources

| Data | Source | Frequency |
|------|--------|----------|
| Home Value Index | CoreLogic | Daily |
| Auction Clearance Rates | CoreLogic | Weekly |
| Housing Finance (lending) | ABS | Monthly |
| Building Approvals | ABS | Monthly |

| Housing Credit Growth | RBA / APRA | Monthly |

## Affordability Benchmarks

| Metric | Sydney | Melbourne | Brisbane | National |
|--------|--------|----------|----------|----------|
| Median Price | $1.2-1.4M | $850-950K | $800-900K | $900K-$1M |
| Price-to-Income | ~12-14x | ~8-10x | ~7-9x | ~9-11x |
| Price-to-Rent | ~30-35x | ~25-28x | ~20-22x | ~27-30x |
| Mortgage as % of Income* | 55-65% | 40-50% | 35-45% | 48-55% |

*At 6.5% rate, 25Y, 20% deposit

## APRA Macroprudential Framework

| Tool | Current | Impact |
|------|---------|--------|
| Interest-Only Lending Cap | Removed (2018, but monitoring) | Was 30% of new lending |
| Investor Lending Growth Cap | Removed (2018) | Was 10% annual limit |
| Debt-to-Income (DTI) | Under consideration | Would cap high-DTI lending |
| Serviceability Buffer | 3% over loan rate | Tightens borrowing capacity |

## Key Risks

### Downside
- Variable rate dominance = severe household stress if rates stay high
- China demand for iron ore declining → WA/QLD mining regions exposed
- Insurance costs rising (flood, bushfire reinsurance)
- High household debt (~200% of disposable income — among highest globally)

### Upside
- Migration-driven demand exceeds supply → floor under prices
- RBA rate cuts (expected 2025) → instant relief to variable-rate borrowers
- 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure pipeline
- Mining supercycle (energy transition metals)

### Cycle Assessment
- Phase: Stabilization → Early Recovery
- Correction depth: Moderate (-5-10% nominal, larger in real terms)
- Key differentiator from NZ: Variable rates = faster pain, but also faster recovery when RBA cuts
- Housing is deeply structurally embedded in Australian economy (~10% of GDP directly, much more via wealth effect)
